## Chapter 1

DARWINISM (1867-1868)

Politics, diplomacy, law, art, and history had opened no outlet for future energy, but a man must do something during long London winters. At that moment Darwin was convulsing society, and his geological champion, Sir Charles Lyell, was intimate at the Legation. Adams was a Darwinist before the letter, a predestined follower of the tide, though hardly trained to follow Darwin's evidences. The atomic theory, the conservation of energy, the mechanical theory of the universe, the kinetic theory of gases, and Natural Selection were examples of what a young man had to take on trust. He was Darwinist because it was easier than not. By rights he should have been a Marxist too, but some narrow trait of the New England nature seemed to blight socialism; he became a Comteist within the limits of evolution.

He never tried to understand Darwin, but fancied he might get the best part of Darwinism from the easier study of geology. Sir Charles in 1866 brought out a new edition of his "Principles." Natural Selection led back to Natural Evolution, and at last to Natural Uniformity—a vast stride. Unbroken Evolution under uniform conditions pleased every one except curates and bishops; it was the very best substitute for religion. When Sir Charles came to the Legation to ask about getting his volume properly noticed in America, young Adams found nothing simpler than to do it himself.

At the very outset he struck on Sir Charles's Glacial Theory. If the glacial period were uniformity, what was catastrophe? Adams hinted his heresies in vain; Sir Charles let the paragraph stand and said not a word. Asked for the simplest case of uniformity on record, Sir Charles named Terebratula, identical from beginning to end of geological time—altogether too much uniformity and far too little selection. Asked then for the first vertebrate, Sir Charles replied that it was a respectable fish whose bones reposed under Adams's own favorite Abbey on Wenlock Edge.

By 1867 Adams knew Shropshire familiarly, and it was the part of his diplomatic education he loved best. He never tired of rambling over the Edge on a summer afternoon, looking across the Marches to the mountains of Wales. The peculiar flavor of the scenery had to do with absence of evolution; one's instinct abhors time. The Roman road was twin to the railroad; one might mix up the terms of time as one liked. But the triumph of all was to look south along the Edge to the abode of one's earliest ancestor and nearest relative, the ganoid fish whose name, according to Professor Huxley, was Pteraspis, a cousin of the sturgeon, and whose kingdom, according to Sir Roderick Murchison, was called Siluria. Behind that horizon lay only the Cambrian, and beyond it the crystalline rocks from which every trace of organic existence had been erased.

Out of his Wenlock musings on Pteraspis Adams carried forward only the suspicion that evolution offered no proof of progress, and that the unity science promised was, like religion, a working hypothesis a historian should accept on faith or not at all.
